articles.summary: Building Freeport Skilled Trades Pipeline, One Intern at a Time mboyle Wed, 09/02/2026 - 09:39 Post Image September 2, 2026 - When Paul Pedrego flipped open an eyewash cover in the company’s Chino mill in New Mexico, he found water but no pressure. He didn’t hesitate. He stopped the work. Pedrego, a Process Automation intern, and his mentor and co-worker, Jose Pacheco, Instrumentation and Control System Electrician, had eight transmitters to calibrate near a bank of reagent flow meters. But as they filled out their job risk assessment, that faulty eyewash station changed the plan. “We both felt it wasn’t safe to continue, so we stopped,” Pedrego said. “This internship taught me a safety culture that’s distinctly Freeport, being your brother’s keeper. It’s not a rule we follow; it’s a responsibility we carry.” Pedrego’s emphasis on safety, and his work the entire summer, didn’t go unnoticed. “I was really glad to have the opportunity to work with Paul,” Pacheco said. “He brings a great attitude to the job, he's a hard worker, and he picks things up incredibly fast. I honestly couldn't ask for a better guy to have on the crew. I'm hoping I get to work with him again soon, and I really hope he decides to bring his talents to Chino operations.” That talent, a summer intern recognizing a risk and willing to stop work, reflects the type of safety-first mindset Freeport strives to foster across its workforce. Freeport recently celebrated and reinforced that commitment at its second annual Skilled Trades Intern Summit in Phoenix. A deliberate strategy Every mill, shop and haul truck at Freeport relies on skilled trades professionals, and the company knows it will need more of them. Launched in 2025, the skilled trades internship program was modeled after Freeport’s university internship program but built for a different purpose: filling the pipeline of frontline talent the business will rely on for decades. “Skilled trades employees are a critical part of our business, and the need for that talent is only growing,” said Alisa Wren, Senior Manager-Talent Acquisition. “This program is about intentionally building that pipeline, investing now in the people who will keep our operations running for years to come.” That strategy already is scaling. In its second year, the program grew to 50 interns from 35 and reached nearly every Freeport operation in the United States, targeting five critical business roles: fixed-plant mechanic, process automation technician, electrical and instrumentation, heavy equipment mechanic, and boilermaker/welder. Many interns come through Freeport’s partnership with Education Forward Arizona, whose Guarantee Your Future program funds scholarships in a designated trade. From last summer’s inaugural class, the company extended offers to eligible interns, with roughly a third converting to full-time employees. Values in the field Rather than the project presentations that anchor the University Intern Conference, the summit was built for connection, pairing interns with the mentors and subject-matter experts who help shape careers in the trades. It’s where strategy meets culture: the pipeline Freeport is building isn’t just technically skilled but grounded in the company’s values. For Wren, the goal is for that momentum to become the norm. “As our sites see the value year over year, my hope is that they’ll fully leverage this program the same way we do for our university interns, a proven pipeline for skilled talent who can build a lasting career with Freeport,” she said. Photos (top and middle): Paul Pedrego (far left), a Process Automation intern at Chino, shares his summer experience alongside fellow interns during a panel at the Skilled Trades Intern Summit in Phoenix; Alisa Wren walks attendees through the program’s reach across Freeport’s United States sites.
articles.title: Building Freeport Skilled Trades Pipeline, One Intern at a Time

articles.summary: Henderson Marks 50 Years of Molybdenum Mining mboyle Wed, 09/16/2026 - 11:59 Post Image September 16, 2026 – Freeport's Henderson mine recently celebrated its 50th anniversary with a sitewide gathering that brought together current employees, retirees and guests to honor five decades of molybdenum production and the people who made it possible. Nestled in the Rocky Mountains, Henderson mine opened in 1976 and quickly established its importance in helping Freeport’s Colorado operations become a global leader in molybdenum production. It also holds the distinction as the company’s only active underground operation in North America. During an afternoon celebration in late August, anniversary activities included lunch, team photos, yard games and guest speakers who shared memories and perspectives on the site’s journey. Employees also were treated to themed chocolates and the opportunity to win commemorative items through raffles and a live auction at the end of the event. For site leaders, the anniversary was not only a celebration of the past, but a reminder of their responsibility to carry that 50-year legacy forward. In his remarks during the event, Climax Molybdenum President Mike Kendrick thanked employees for continuing a culture of excellence that has defined Henderson for decades. Honoring Legacy “I am personally inspired by the dedication shown by everyone involved, both past and present,” Kendrick said. “Your commitment today ensures our continued success and honors the legacy built by those who came before us. I encourage everyone to reflect on their own experiences at Freeport, Climax Molybdenum and Henderson, and to take pride in the collective achievements that have shaped our organization.” That commitment has molded an operation that never stood still. Over the decades, Henderson continually has adapted its equipment and practices to meet changing needs, and employees who once relied on the “Loci” rail system to move ore watched it give way to the now-iconic, miles-long conveyor network, reflecting the broader transformation of the operation over the past half century. The changes extend well beyond material handling. Above ground, crews are advancing construction of a new water treatment plant, while development work continues on new mining panels underground, drawing upon decades of experience even as it continues to adapt. While the anniversary highlighted how much Henderson has changed, a number of employees pointed to something that has remained remarkably consistent: its culture. Reconnecting with the Past The celebration drew not only current employees, but also retirees eager to reconnect with former coworkers and revisit a place that helped shape their careers. Some traveled long distances to attend, underscoring the lasting bonds formed at Henderson over the past five decades. Among those in attendance was engineer John Barnes, one of the many employees who witnessed Henderson’s progress firsthand. Retired for more than a decade now, Barnes said the culture at Henderson has stuck with him and helped it stand apart from his other jobs. “I loved it here and I still love it here,” Barnes said. “It wasn’t about your office or what view you had out of your window. It was about how you contribute to a team effort and do something meaningful, like extracting a mineral out of the ground that the world needs.” Photos (top and middle): Anna Cable, Senior Operational Excellence Engineer, enjoyed some of the yard games before the main event; Henderson’s 50th anniversary celebration featured a number of speakers, including Climax Molybdenum President Mike Kendrick.
articles.title: Henderson Marks 50 Years of Molybdenum Mining

articles.summary: AIM Fellows Complete Summer Experience mboyle Thu, 09/24/2026 - 12:09 Post Image September 24, 2026 - A dozen college educators representing schools across the country are back on campus and better positioned to discuss the intricacies of mining with their students. A group of 12 higher education faculty members recently completed Freeport’s Academic-Industry Mining (AIM) Fellowship, an experiential learning opportunity intended to provide participants firsthand insight into modern mining practices they can bring back into the classroom. Through the program, educators spent at least six weeks working alongside Freeport employees, contributing to projects aligned with their academic interests. The fellowship is designed not only to provide practical industry experience but also to help those educators better prepare the next generation of mining professionals. The goal of this program is to help create “a pipeline to our future workforce,” said Angie Harmon, Regional Manager of Social Performance-North America. This year, the groundwork for that pipeline was laid with the help of 12 educators from universities across the U.S., including Kate Brown Requist, an assistant professor of mining engineering at Tennessee State University, and Azeem Raza, an assistant research professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology. Other participating universities included Arizona State University, Colorado School of Mines, Michigan Technological University, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, University of Arizona and West Virginia University. In addition to working on projects related to their own areas of expertise, the fellows also had the opportunity to visit Freeport operations and meet with employees across the business. Those experiences included attending a Reinvent Mining meeting in Phoenix and a visit to Tucson, where they toured the Technology Center and Sierrita mine, getting a closer look at the processes and technology behind the mining industry today. Brown Requist said the opportunity offered a valuable look at just how much Freeport is helping shape the future of the mining industry. “It was very eye-opening,” Brown Requist said. “There’s a lot going on at Freeport, and this was an opportunity to see what that leading edge of innovation looks like and how the company is leveraging analytics. It’s a great example to show my students what modernizing and digitizing the mining industry really looks like.” Raza’s opportunities were more connected to the company’s innovation deployment. With an interest in how mine design will evolve and adopt technologies like artificial intelligence, automation and robotics as they become more specialized and commonplace in mining, Raza was given the opportunity to visit the company’s Bagdad mine, where he saw firsthand how Freeport is leading the industry’s adoption of autonomous haulage in the U.S. “Bagdad is a very exciting location,” Raza said. “It is clear Freeport is looking to the future and is optimizing its operations for that. Autonomous haulage, robotics, artificial intelligence – these are the topics that should attract the next generation, and now I can help prepare them to contribute more significantly.” Photos (top and bottom): Kate Brown Requist got a closer look at Arizona’s geology during a visit to the company’s Sierrita mine; During their time with Freeport, Azeem Raza and the other fellows toured the labs at Technology Center Tucson.
articles.title: AIM Fellows Complete Summer Experience

articles.summary: Boris Medina’s Leadership Recognized with Regional Award mboyle Mon, 09/21/2026 - 12:04 Post Image September 21, 2026 - El Abra President Boris Medina recently received the Radoslav Razmilic Award, which recognizes executives who have made significant contributions to strengthening industry and advancing the development of the Antofagasta region in Chile. The award is presented by the Antofagasta Industrial Association (AIA), one of the leading business organizations in northern Chile. The association brings together companies connected to mining and productive development in the Antofagasta region where El Abra operates. Medina is a member of the AIA Board of Directors. The recognition coincides with El Abra’s 30th anniversary. It also comes as the company is advancing its Operational Continuity Project, which is intended to extend the mine life by more than four decades. “This recognition is especially meaningful because it reflects the work of the teams I have had the opportunity to collaborate with throughout my career,” Medina said. “It also represents El Abra’s commitment to the development of mining and the communities of the Antofagasta Region, an effort we have built together with our employees, partners and neighboring communities for more than 30 years.” Photo: El Abra President Boris Medina, center, recently received the Radoslav Razmilic Award.
articles.title: Boris Medina’s Leadership Recognized with Regional Award
